articles.title: Jess Cartner-Morley on fashion: pair a little skirt with a chunky jumper for the perfect balancing act
articles.summary: Let your legs enjoy the last of the summer’s breeze while a thick top or jacket keeps away the autumn chill. This is the most enjoyable time of the year to get dressed because clothes can just be clothes.
body: And this benign early part of autumn is more fun to dress for than the equivalent weather in spring, because we still have a bit of summer swagger. The summer habit of wearing shorts and halter tops and even swimwear has gotten us a little loose, a little more laid-back about flashing a bit of skin here or there. It is about more than bare flesh, though. There is something about summer that flexes the flashy dresser in everyone – whether that’s fancy dress for a festival, or just the way that putting on a pair of sunglasses brings out your inner movie star.

It is very important to hold on to that summer glow, that more fabulous version of yourself, the one who starred in your holiday snaps carousel, for as long as you can. I do this literally, getting through my bodyweight in Dove Visible Glow, my preferred slap-it-on-like-body-lotion gradual self-tan, between now and when the clocks go back. But the less literal-minded among you can hold on to that lovely golden-hour feeling in your mind, as well as in your body. Stay locked into your summer playlist and keep hold of that windows-down, shades-on spirit of freedom at least until the leaves start to turn.

articles.title: ‘We thought death could do with a bit of dancing’: welcome to Sondering, the arts festival with its own funeral march
articles.summary: A brush with mortality inspired sisters Sophia and Camilla Minden to create a death-themed event featuring live bands, wild swimming … and an ‘emoshpit’ Raised in the Lake District on “music, moss and macaroni cheese,” Sophia and Camilla Minden were mindful of death from a very early age.
body: What they didn’t expect was that little more than a decade later, they’d be planning Camilla’s own funeral. Diagnosed with late-stage Hodgkin’s lymphoma just after her 20th birthday, she was given an 80% chance of survival, but the other 20% made her investigate her local undertakers (“dated, impersonal and expensive”) and work out what she wanted at her funeral (“spag bol and quite a lot of Michael Jackson”). Navigating “shit wigs” and people’s awkwardness around the subject of dying, she says that she spent a lot of time “bargaining with God”, promising that if she made it through, she’d live life to the full and appreciate every single day.

articles.title: Hoy Is Bringing Night-Market Energy to NYC
articles.summary: This excerpt was originally published in Pre Shift, our newsletter for the hospitality industry. Subscribe for more first-person accounts, advice, and interviews. This is the first installment of our series Getting on the Map, presented by Apple Maps.
body: When I spoke with Cyed Adraincem, he apologized for stumbling over any words; he’d been up at 4 a.m. to wash the sidewalk in front of his forthcoming restaurant. “I wanted to beat all the foot traffic,” he said.

Adraincem seems to have brought that same dedication to outfitting Hoy, which will serve Filipino street food in a Manila night-market-like space. Though not yet open, the restaurant has already garnered a lot of attention for its loud and off-kilter aesthetic, smart pop cultural ties, and behind-the-scenes peeks into R&D. I asked him about designing the space, the merch plan, and how opening is going.

Cyed Adraincem: It’s Filipino street food, super fast casual. I’m trying to introduce Filipino food to a broader audience because I feel like we’re underrepresented in New York City. We’ll be serving barbecue skewers, lumpia, and a couple different sandwiches. It’s a pretty simple menu, nothing too fancy, mostly traditional, with chef techniques that we’ve learned over the years. I think the New York dining scene wants something more casual, more affordable right now. They don’t want something pretentious; they just want to eat and have a good drink.

articles.title: Sali Hughes on beauty: lip gloss is back in vogue and these new formulas have me hooked
articles.summary: Personally, I’ve never been a fan of painting on the gloss, but thanks to a range of fresh formats in sophisticated shades and textures, my head – and lips – have been turned. I’m deeply suspicious of people who never change their minds.
body: I do the same with lip gloss, with historically similar results. Fashion has, until recently, been on my side. Less sophisticated than lipstick, overshadowed by TikTok trending lip oils, less effortless cool-girl than tinted lip balm, gloss has barely had a look-in these past few years, but new formulas steal from other formats for a better user experience and, well, like everything eventually, lip gloss is back in vogue.

The launch of Nars’ Afterglow Lipshine (£28.50) was what first got me hooked. Its smooth, unsticky texture, lack of scent and lasting moisture make it a pleasure, and a characteristically thoughtful colour range makes the whole lineup feel as adult and sophisticated as lipstick.

Smooth Talk, a cool, sheer cocoa brown, was my most worn lip colour of last winter (either alone or over lipstick) and will soon see me through another. I’ll be adding in Nympho, an unusual cool taupe. Abbey Road, a golden, shimmering (who even am I?) bronze has lived in my handbag all summer, alongside a nude lip liner and … not one lipstick.

articles.title: Why Would Fashion Ever Ban Sheep Wool?
articles.summary: Having moved the needle on fur and leather, Peta protestors are now calling on fashion to phase out sheep wool from clothing. But questions remain over whether the industry could — and should — do so.
body: It’s a complicated question. Animal rights activists argue that even the strictest certifications can’t stamp out rough handling and inhumane conditions entirely. But, unlike virgin animal fur and leather, the conversation around banning wool is nearly non-existent. In fact, knitwear is booming. And the International Woolmark Prize — which encourages emerging designers to explore the creative potential of Australian wool — is one of fashion’s leading talent incubators, counting Jean Paul Gaultier creative director Duran Lantink as its most recent winner and Karl Lagerfeld, Valentino Garavani and Yves Saint Laurent among its earliest (Woolmark does not comment on Peta activations).

articles.title: Kim Kardashian and Ludovic de Saint Sernin Will Release a Skims Collaboration
articles.summary: “The pieces we made are really classic and simple designs,” says Kardashian. “It has the Ludovic sex element to it, mixed with the simplicity of Skims.”
body: Kardashian has since worn de Saint Sernin on countless occasions—slipping into everything from his crochet bikini tops to extreme ripped jeans. So perhaps it’s no great surprise that, almost a decade later, the pair is expanding their personal relationship into a creative partnership: Today, the pair announces Skims x Ludovic de Saint Sernin, a collaboration coming later this fall. “The conversation has always been open on working together,” says Kardashian, who founded her own brand, Skims, in 2019. “That’s always been a part of our love language: How can we have fun and elevate each other?”

The collection will take cues from ’90s supermodel style—offering slinky pieces that are imbued with a sense of power and strength—but will also draw from Kardashian’s own archive of looks. “All of her different eras inspired me for this collection,” says de Saint Sernin. “I was going through her archive, and things that I loved seeing on her. We just wanted pieces that enhance the body and make people feel confident. That’s something we share in common: Celebrating the body in every shape and form.”

articles.title: Exclusive: Lena Dunham Is a Mother! The Sweet, Singular Story of How She Prepared
articles.summary: Anxiously awaiting the birth of her child via surrogate, Lena Dunham turned to one thing she could control: building the infant wardrobe of her dreams.
body: It was a mild November morning when I found myself kneeling by an exam table, fresh off a red-eye—with a rictus grin of anxious enthusiasm plastered on the lower half of my face while my eyes filled with anxious tears—clutching the hand of a woman I had met in person only twice.

While I’ve been known to make friends quickly—​airport terminals, veterinary offices—​this was the quickest leap from first coffee to gynecological procedure I’d ever done. And in that moment, as we watched the ball of cells our doctor had already told us could someday form a girl shooting across the dark ultrasound screen like a UFO on a mission, I had the overwhelming urge to tell her I loved her. Babies and dogs, they’ll coax it out of you fast.
